clinicalPearls: A congenital vascular malformation producing a fixed, reticulated, marbled (livedoid) violaceous pattern of the skin present from birth
The mottling is persistent and does not fully resolve on warming, distinguishing it from benign physiological cutis marmorata
It often has a segmental or localised distribution, and the affected area may show mild atrophy, ulceration or dilated superficial veins
A degree of limb or body asymmetry (hypoplasia or, less often, hypertrophy) can accompany the skin changes
It is usually sporadic and tends to improve gradually over the first years of life
Associated anomalies are described, including glaucoma when facial skin around the eye is involved, so ophthalmology assessment is warranted in periocular disease
Diagnosis is clinical; imaging is reserved for evaluating associated limb asymmetry or other suspected anomalies
Management is largely supportive, with monitoring of associated features and protection of atrophic or ulcerated skin
reference.pathophysiology: Cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita is a sporadic congenital malformation of the cutaneous microvasculature in which persistently dilated capillaries and venules produce a fixed reticulated, marbled discolouration of the skin. The affected vessels and surrounding dermis may be structurally abnormal, accounting for associated skin atrophy, ulceration and prominent superficial veins. The underlying cause is not fully defined and most cases occur without a clear inheritance pattern; the reticulated pattern tends to soften with time as the microvasculature matures.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal lupus and other neonatal livedo
Adams-Oliver syndrome (with aplasia cutis and limb defects)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination documenting the fixed reticulated pattern and its distribution
Ophthalmological assessment for glaucoma when periocular skin is involved
Limb-length and girth measurement to assess asymmetry
Imaging (ultrasound or MRI) if significant limb asymmetry or other anomaly is suspected
Skin assessment for atrophy or ulceration
Developmental review where broader syndromic features are present
redFlags: Periocular involvement with signs of raised intraocular pressure or glaucoma
Persistent ulceration or non-healing skin breakdown
Features suggesting an associated syndrome requiring further workup
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous mottling commonly fades and improves over the first few years of life, and isolated disease has a good prognosis; outlook is determined by any associated anomalies such as glaucoma or substantial limb asymmetry, which require targeted follow-up.
pitfalls: Confusing it with benign physiological cutis marmorata that resolves on warming
Omitting ophthalmology review when the skin around the eye is affected
Overlooking limb asymmetry that may need orthopaedic follow-up
Assuming all cases are isolated without checking for associated anomalies
references: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Haemangiomas and Malformations
management: Conservative management with reassurance, as the mottling commonly fades over the first years of life and no specific therapy is required
Ophthalmology assessment and glaucoma screening with intraocular pressure monitoring when periocular skin is involved
Monitoring of limb length and girth for asymmetry, with orthopaedic input and leg-length correction where needed
Skin care and treatment of any atrophy or ulceration of affected areas
Pulsed-dye laser for persistent, cosmetically troublesome lesions
Care through a vascular anomalies multidisciplinary team with developmental review where broader syndromic features are present
